## Researcher Response 39

**All ten ordinary surfaces are conservative in every dimension on a finite 3-computad if each generating 3-cell has a generating variable as target.** The 2-skeleton is arbitrary. In particular its 2-generators can have composite or identity boundaries, and a 3-rule can merge an entire diagram of 2-cells. The same result holds with source and target interchanged throughout the top declarations.

More generally let $B$ be any finite ordinary $n$-computad, $n\ge2$. Form $D$ by adjoining $(n+1)$-generators $z:s_z\to g_z$ where $g_z$ is literally an $n$-variable and $s_z$ is any parallel raw term. Fix one of the eight binary or two published surfaces. In each degree $k$, conservativity on $B$ implies conservativity on $D$. For $k\ge n+2$ the implication is an equivalence. For $k\ge n+3$ even the assertion that **every** raw $k$-type is inhabited passes from $B$ to $D$. All three statements have the single-source dual. We first give the raw mapping-space argument that allows the lower skeleton to be arbitrary.

### A fresh target with a specified incoming arrow

Start with $B$ and form a finite sequence $C$ of pairs of declarations. At each step take an already formed $n$-term $s$, introduce a **fresh** $n$-variable $t$ of its type, and introduce $z:s\to t$. Later pairs may use $t$ repeatedly. Write $i:B\to C$ for inclusion. There is a raw substitution $e:C\to B$ (in the direction of maps of free algebras) fixing $B$, sending $t$ to $e(s)$ and $z$ to $1_{e(s)}$. It is well typed since the added $n$-variable has exactly the type of $s$.

Realize these computads as in Response 36. Fix a raw boundary below degree $n$ and take its iterated hom. Denote the resulting $(\infty,1)$-categories by $H_B,H_C$, so $n$-cells at these poles give objects, and $(n+1)$-cells give morphisms. The lower poles are in the common skeleton. For $x\in H_B$ and $y\in H_C$ the induced map is an equivalence of spaces
$$
 e:\operatorname{Map}_{H_C}(i x,y)\ \longrightarrow\
       \operatorname{Map}_{H_B}(x,e y).                                      \tag{3}
$$
It suffices to construct, on each such hom, a natural transformation $\eta:ie\Rightarrow 1$ that restricts to the identity on $iH_B$. To do so take the arrow category $\operatorname{Fun}([1],-)$ in the *innermost* enrichment direction. This functor preserves cartesian products, with evaluation at either end and the constant-arrow functor product-preserving as well. Applying it to hom objects and their composition, and iterating the change of enrichment through the $n$ outer directions, defines an $(\infty,n+1)$-category with these arrow categories as its fixed iterated homs. One may take the same objects at each enriched step before completion. Completion is fully faithful on homs at those objects. Thus a map into this target gives ordinary natural transformations on the fixed homs, compatible with composition in the other directions. [Haugseng, comparison with iterated enrichment](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.3881) · [Cellular realization and fixed homs](#researcher-response-36)

On $B$ take the constant arrows on $i$. Suppose the map has been constructed through the preceding pairs, with evaluations $ie$ and the inclusion there. Its value on $s$ is an arrow $\eta_s:ie(s)\to s$. Assign to the new $t$ the composite $z\circ\eta_s$. To the new $z$ assign the square from $\eta_s$ to this composite with sides $1_{ie(s)}$ and $z$. A compositional triangle of the pair $(\eta_s,z)$ provides precisely this square, including the identity side. These are cells in the same iterated hom, since $s,t$ have the same actual lower type. The cellular pushout for the pair extends the map with the specified evaluations, up to homotopy relative to the preceding stage. Explicitly the new object and its incoming arrow in the arrow category are the chosen composite and square. Their endpoint diagrams are $(ie(s),1_{ie(s)})$ and $(t,z)$, the two required attaching diagrams. Induction constructs $\eta$, with the endpoint identifications relative to $B$.

Postcomposing $i(p)$ with $\eta_y$ gives a map back in (3). Its composite after $e$ on the left-hand mapping space is homotopic to the identity by naturality and $\eta_{ix}=1$. Its composite on the right-hand space is postcomposition with $e(\eta_y)$. This is an equivalence because $B$ has generators only through degree $n$, so its innermost hom at these poles is a space. Together these two calculations prove (3). In particular the calculation respects all higher homotopies and applies at any prescribed parallel faces in the mapping space. It uses a directed arrow $z$ only in its declared direction.

The degree $n+1$ argument also gives an exact test at an individual raw boundary $x\to v$. Starting at any finite ordinary 2-computad and iterating these extensions gives all ten conservativity assertions in all dimensions. The orientation can be chosen separately at each new degree. ### A gluing condition equivalent to the unrestricted ordinary question

Fix one surface and one output degree $k$. Consider the following restricted family of pushouts of finite presentations. Start with an $n$-computad $B$, $n\ge2$, and a finite list of parallel pairs $s_j,t_j$ of $n$-terms. Add to $B$ a fresh $n$-variable $w_j$ of their common type for every pair, obtaining $B'$. Over $B'$ one side $D_-$ freely adds just $a_j:s_j\to w_j$. The other side $D_+$ freely adds just $b_j:w_j\to t_j$. The two sides use the same indexed variables, and the original attaching terms use none of them.

The universal ordinary assertion in degree $k$ is **equivalent** to closure of conservativity in that degree under precisely these pushouts: if $B',D_-,D_+$ are conservative, so is $D_-\amalg_{B'}D_+$. In one direction this follows immediately from universality. For the other, use induction on generating dimension, starting with Response 10. Given an $(n+1)$-computad $X$, take $B=X_{\le n}$ and the actual top declarations $z_j:s_j\to t_j$. The induction hypothesis gives conservativity on $B'$, which still has dimension at most $n$. The two orientations of the theorem give it on $D_-$ and $D_+$. The closure hypothesis gives it on their pushout $P$.

Map $X$ into $P$ by the identity on $B$ and the top composite of $a_j,b_j$ at $z_j$. A raw return sends $w_j$ to $s_j$, $a_j$ to $1_{s_j}$, and $b_j$ to $z_j$. The round trip on $z_j$ is the left-unit padding of $z_j$. Its raw unitor gives an invertible comparison relative to the two original faces. These comparisons give a homotopy of the two maps $X\to X$ relative to $B$: the space of maps out of this cellular extension with the base map fixed is the product of the spaces of fillers at the individual attaching boundaries, and the unit comparison is a path in each such space. Thus raw inhabitation reflects at every translated old type by the globe restriction fibration. Every surface inhabitant translates along the forward substitution. A failure in $X$ would give one in $P$, proving the induction. In particular, if a universal case fails, there is a failing pushout of this form with both pieces and their intersection conservative in the failing degree. This isolates the remaining gluing question even for contexts with identities in both faces of an original declaration. [Reflection at a prescribed type under a homotopy retraction](#researcher-response-24) ∎

## Researcher Response 40

**For both kernels, any failure in a source-positive computad is already a failure at the universal strict cell of a single finite polyplex, with the weak attaching terms lifted from the given computad.** In the lifted problem there is no raw filler at its old boundary, even if one allows any strict value. Above the generating dimension this also gives a criterion in the opposite direction for an individual context. The statements apply to all eight binary surfaces and to both published ordinary theories. One may independently specify source- or target-positivity in each rank. Here positivity on a chosen side means that the ordinary strict face on that side of each generator of degree at least two is a nonidentity cell in the immediately preceding dimension. No bound is imposed on the lengths of these faces.

### Lifting the strict labelling of a whole derivation

Write $F$ for the **ordinary** free strict image throughout, including for Gray input. Let $L_X$ mean the free algebra of the selected theory on the raw declarations of $X$; we may select either raw theory itself as well. Let $f:Y\to X$ preserve generators and their actual attaching terms. Suppose the strict functor $Ff$ has the following properties.

* A specified identity or binary composite in the image of a cell lifts uniquely as that identity or as a composable pair above the specified two factors, at every compositional cut.
* Every strict preimage of a generating cell of $X$ in its own degree is a generating cell of $Y$.

The first condition is the discrete Conduché lifting property. Then, in **every** degree, the canonical map is an isomorphism of globular sets
$$
                 L_Y\ \longrightarrow\ L_X\times_{F(X)}F(Y).                  \tag{4}
$$
For the raw theories these are literal terms. For the surfaces these are conversion classes. In particular the statement records the lift of the entire term at its specified strict value, not just the existence of a term at some boundary.

Here are the details for passing from globular generators to arbitrary attaching types. On globular input write $L(Z)$ and $F(Z)$ for the corresponding free algebras. The map $L(Z)\to F(Z)$ is cartesian in globular maps $Z\to Z'$ by Responses 4, 27 and 32. In particular use $Z\to 1$, with $1$ the terminal globular set. An operation is given by its generic operation on its positional tree and a labelling of precisely that tree: the strict cell in $F(Z)$ supplies the tree and its labels, and its image in $L(1)$ supplies the operation there by the same pullback. Composition of operations substitutes the trees, since the strict projection commutes with substitution. This describes operations **after** all equations of the selected theory; it applies also to generic head types formed using conversion. [Raw positional lifting](#researcher-response-4) · [Published comparison](#researcher-response-27) · [Binary comparison](#researcher-response-32)

Regard $P=F(X)$ and $Q=F(Y)$ as algebras of this theory by strict evaluation. Pullback of algebras along $Q\to P$ preserves colimits in the slice. To verify this, let $A\to Q$ be an algebra over $Q$. Define a right adjoint as follows. Over a $j$-cell $p$ of $P$, choose parallel boundary families already defined over its two faces, and for each $q$ over $p$ choose a cell in $A$ over $q$ with faces the entries at the two faces of $q$. In degree zero there is just the family of entries. Keeping the boundary families separately handles empty fibres. For a labelled operation over $P$ and a specified strict lift of its result, split that lift over the entire strict positional tree of the operation. Choose any composition expression for the tree, use unique binary lifts and lift the identity paddings. The resulting labels are compatible on incident faces. Equivalently, restriction of strict labellings of the tree to its two pasted pieces is bijective onto pairs agreeing on their common boundary, and the unique lifts give just such a pair. Splitting is independent of the expression: an associativity, unit or exchange step composes the already lifted factors on its other side, with uniqueness recovering the same factors on decomposing back. This includes whiskerings by identities and steps inside a larger expression. Thus restriction to a face gives its split, and splitting a substitution in two stages gives the split on the substituted tree. Evaluate the operation in $A$ on the family entries at these lifted labels. The face, identity and composition checks follow from these split identities and the algebra laws in $A$. This gives the family algebra over $P$. A map over $Q$ from the pullback of an algebra $M\to P$ to $A$ is exactly a map over $P$ from $M$ to these families: evaluate or collect at $(m,q)$. The same split formula verifies that either passage preserves operations. This proves the slice adjunction and colimit preservation.

Compute the pullback of the cellular presentation of $L_X$ in that slice. For one generator $b$ of degree $j$, let $G$ be its formal globular $j$-disc, and consider $L(G)\to P$ given by $b$. The strict pullback $F(G)\times_P Q$ is free on the globular set $Z$ of pairs consisting of a generating disc position and a strict lift of its assigned label; that label can be a composite on a proper face. By the globular comparison, the algebra pullback of $L(G)$ is $L(Z)$. Relative to the pulled-back boundary it freely attaches one $j$-cell for every strict lift of $b$. These lifts are exactly its generating preimages by the second hypothesis. Induct on the cellular presentation. At the preceding stage the actual raw attaching faces of each such generator have the required two projections, its lifted strict faces and the old attaching expressions of $b$. By the preceding pullback isomorphism they are exactly the attaching faces in this pushout. Thus every stage attaches precisely the generators of $Y$ over that stage with their given weak boundaries. This computes the whole pullback and proves (4).

### A positive strict cell and its weak attaching terms

For a source-positive strict polygraph, Henry associates to each ordinary strict cell $c$ a finite polyplex $P_c$ with universal cell $\gamma$ and a generator-preserving labelling $P_c\to X$ representing $c$. The representation is unique up to unique isomorphism of the polyplex **with its cell**. In a specified composite the representing object is the pushout of the factor polyplexes along the polyplex of their common face. Consequently generator-preserving maps between source-positive polygraphs have both hypotheses of (4). To lift a specified factorization restrict the representing labelling upstairs to each piece of that pushout. Conversely compatible restrictions glue uniquely. An identity has the same representing diagram as the cell it pads, and the polyplex representing a generator is a plex with its universal generator; all its labellings send that position to a generator. Global strict opposites can be taken independently in each positive dimension: reversing the arrows in degree $j$ switches the two $(j-1)$-faces of every $j$-generator and preserves whether either is an identity. Applying the chosen involution to the strict diagram, doing the calculation, and undoing it gives the same representation and factor lifting for every choice of side per rank. This invokes opposites only in ordinary **strict** categories, so no invariance of directed Gray syntax under these operations is needed. [Henry, §§2.2.6, 2.2.9, Corollary 2.3.12 and Theorem 2.4.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00744)

There is a canonical choice of **raw** presentation of $P_c$ relative to the labelling and the given raw $X$. In rank zero keep its vertices. For a generating position labelled $b$, lift the two actual terms in the attaching type of $b$ at the strict values of the two faces of that position. Apply the raw version of (4) on the already constructed lower skeleta. The two lifted faces are literally parallel because their own faces lift identical terms at identical strict values. This defines the next weak declaration. Induction gives a finite presentation $\widetilde P_c$ and a map $f:\widetilde P_c\to X$ preserving the actual declarations. It also proves uniqueness over this particular labelling. Identity padding of $c$ to a higher output degree pads $\gamma$ at the same generating diagram.

Now let a surface judgement at a prescribed old boundary in $X$ have strict value $c$. Lift its cell along $f$ at $\gamma$ by (4), and its old faces by the raw version at the faces of $\gamma$. Parallelism is literal, and these are the faces of the lifted surface cell after passage to its surface class, by uniqueness in (4). Any raw filler of this lifted boundary folds to a raw filler in $X$. Hence a failure in $X$ is a failure on this one $\widetilde P_c$, allowing all candidate raw fillers there. In particular the universal question within each indicated class of finite computads is equivalent to testing its polyplex presentations at such universal values. The proof retains the weak writings of the declarations even where full strict-image conversion fails on the underlying positive polyplex.

For an individual $X$, raw and surface fillers of a **specified** strict value $c$ correspond bijectively to fillers of value $\gamma$ at that lifted boundary, separately for each theory. The lifted presentation has dimension less than $k$ too, so its lifted old faces likewise admit only that identity value for a filler. It follows that conservativity in this degree on $X$ holds exactly when it holds on all these lifted boundary problems over its labelled polyplexes. In lower degrees a different strict $k$-cell at the same boundary can supply a raw filler in $X$, which the fixed-value bijection handles by testing the other labels separately.

### The mapping space of a pair of paths

Write $A,B$ for the free categories on $L,R$, and $I,J$ for their discrete object categories. In the fixed outer hom from 0 to 3, take the further hom between the opposite 1-paths $f_0gh_0,f_1gh_1$. Its objects are the corners $(i,j)$. As an $(\infty,1)$-category this hom is
$$
 V=(A\times B)\amalg_K(A\times B),\qquad
 K=(A\times J)\amalg_{I\times J}(I\times B).                       \tag{5}
$$
All pushouts here are derived. Indeed, in the enriched outer line, the two intervals supporting the new rules are $[0,2]$ and $[1,3]$. They cannot both occur as separate factors of an outer composition. On the first interval the inner walking family of arrows indexed by $I$ becomes the two-object category enriched with forward hom $A$; likewise for $B$ on the second interval. At $[0,3]$ take the pushout of the two extensions, each multiplied by the unchanged family at its exterior edge. The inner objects form a square with four side homs $A,B,A,B$. The colimit of the input diagonals is $K$. There are precisely two compositions via a middle object. For each one the old product of sides contributes $K$ and the product of the resulting sides is $A\times B$. The attaching map from the two old copies of $K$ is the fold. This gives (5) by the same enriched universal property as for the circle. Even if the graphs have loops, nonempty words in a free category are never invertible, so these side categories add no equivalences of lower objects. All other nonidentity fixed homs at this depth are free path categories or discrete categories, as one reads from the shorter intervals or sides of this square. The strict comparison on (5) records just the pair of paths in $A,B$.

Fix such a pair $(p,q)$ of lengths $m,n$, counting occurrences even when labels repeat. The space of 3-cells over this pair, with its lower poles fixed, has the following cubical model. Its vertices shuffle the two lists in their given internal orders. Two adjacent unlike entries can switch in **two** ways, one for each sheet of (5). Any collection of disjoint adjacent switches spans a cube for every choice of their sheets.

To derive this model, present each free category by its vertices and a copy of $\Delta^1$ for each generating edge. Cartesian product in $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$ preserves colimits separately. Thus (5) attaches two copies of the simplicial square for each pair of edges to the grid graph, identifying their perimeters, also when endpoints of generating edges agree. Equivalently use simplicial sets: attaching a generating interval or a square along its boundary is a homotopy pushout since the boundary inclusion is a cofibration and the objects are cofibrant. In simplicial rigidification the two triangles in each square adjoin a diagonal arrow and intervals from the two serial routes to that diagonal. More explicitly the image of $\Delta^2$ has an interval from the direct edge to its factorization at the middle vertex. Rigidification preserves these attaching colimits. In a fixed mapping space the words can consequently contain single steps, one of the two diagonal arrows for a pair, or one of the comparisons between a diagonal and its two-step route. Simultaneous intervals in a word occur exactly on disjoint blocks. Composition concatenates words. Hence these products of intervals subdivide exactly the stated cubes, with one subdivision vertex on each switch edge. Fixing the two projected words indexes every occurrence even in a loop; no quotient by permutations of equal names is taken. [Dugger–Spivak, rigidification and the mapping simplicial sets of a simplex](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.0814)

This complex is connected by sorting. Its vertex links are flag: choices of directions span a simplex precisely when their adjacent pairs are pairwise disjoint, with at most one choice at each pair. The complex is nonpositively curved by the cubical link criterion, so each such space is aspherical. Its fundamental group has a presentation with a generator $t_{ij}$ for each crossing of the $i$th letter of $p$ and the $j$th of $q$, and only the relations
$$
                  [t_{ij},t_{kl}]=1 \qquad(i<k,\ j<l).              \tag{6}
$$
To see this, orient a switch by moving the right-list letter to the left. Starting with all of $p$ first, the resulting inversion sets are ideals of the rectangular poset (decreasing left index and increasing right index). The subcomplex using only the first-sheet edges is simply connected: every monotone path to an ideal is a linear extension of that ideal, and interchanging incomparable consecutive moves is a square. Choosing these paths from the initial word trivializes every first-sheet edge in the fundamental groupoid. An oriented edge on the other sheet now gives one generator for its pair, independent of the enabling ideal. Indeed the enabling ideals contain all strict predecessors of the pair, omit it and its successors, and are connected by moves incomparable to it. Slide the edge along those moves by mixed-sheet squares. Two other-sheet edges span a square exactly for incomparable pairs, giving (6). Conversely label the first edges by 1 and the second by the indicated letters in (6); all squares commute there. This verifies that there are no further relations. In particular all well-formed old types of degree at least six in these contexts already have raw fillers, by asphericity and the exact globe-fibre test. This statement concerns a word on the generic globular set. An arbitrary declared $l$-cell in a computad can have composite faces.

This terminates by rank after finite syntactic unification at each stage. A solution of the constraints gives the requested representative by substitution. ### Encoding reachability at the one fixed reverse type

Take finite substring rules on an alphabet, with nonempty sides, and nonempty words $u,v$. Reachability in such systems is undecidable, already using both orientations of the relations of a finitely presented semigroup. Add two fresh markers $L,R$. These placements form a finite list: split the temporal history into prefix, generator window and suffix, match the declaration's spatial path at a contiguous position on the actual edge path before the window, and compare the positions and names in that window. An empty spatial path matches at its vertex. Shift each crossing in the two faces by the temporal prefix length. Discard placements outside the retained graph. Every whole-path rewrite is $p l q\to p r q$, where $p:D\to u$ and $q:t(l)\to E$. This description permits declarations on smaller windows and arbitrary changes in crossing length. Response 48 proves the equality of this reachability test with raw inhabitation at the given old faces.

In the two-cycle case encode a whole path by its residual path and the numbers of complete turns at $D$ and at $E$. Strip the maximal complete initial turns based at $D$ and the maximal complete terminal turns based at $E$. There are finitely many residual paths: the middle graph is acyclic and both leftover cycle segments have bounded length. To compile $l\to r$, enumerate *simple* paths $p,q$ at its two sides, allowing the empty ones. If $p l q$ has code $(s,i,j)$ and $p r q$ has code $(t,i',j')$, introduce the move
$$
 (s,i+m,j+n)\longrightarrow(t,i'+m,j'+n)\qquad(m,n\ge0).
$$
These moves are exact. Erasing a complete turn in a general $p$ or $q$ changes the two whole paths by a common exterior turn. Indeed inside a simple cycle, a turn followed by a segment equals that segment followed by a turn based at its other end. A path cannot leave the component and return to it. This moves all erased turns to $D$ or $E$. Conversely any number of such exterior turns are legal on both whole paths. The resulting finite-control two-counter system is decidable by the path-scheme algorithm of Response 48.

In the one-cycle case choose a vertex $v$ on the cycle. A path missing $v$ has its literal finite-control code and count zero. For a path visiting $v$, retain its prefix up to the first visit and its suffix from the last visit. Count the intervening complete turns. Both retained segments have bounded length because the graph off $v$ is acyclic. In compiling the contextual moves now enumerate $p,q$ visiting $v$ at most once each. If either visits $v$, arbitrary additional turns can be inserted there on both sides of the rewrite. The compiled move sends $i+m$ to $i'+m$ for every $m\ge0$, with the corresponding change of finite control. If neither visits $v$, it applies **only at $i$**, with output $i'$. This exhausts all contexts by stripping turns in $p,q$ separately. In particular an occurrence lying inside the face $l$ does not by itself permit a turn to be added in the outside context.

For completeness the exact-value test needs only a one-symbol stack with a bottom test. Pop the required count, test for empty in the exact case, then push the output count, using private intermediate states. Push the initial count at entry and pop the target count at exit. Compute the empty-to-empty balanced relation without zero tests by closing identity and neutral edges under concatenation and under a push followed by a balanced path followed by a pop. This finite relation accounts for every such path by splitting at the match of its first push. At height zero take the transitive closure of the balanced relation and the empty tests. Splitting at visits to those tests proves exactness for the full system.

### The undecidable case with different names

At a common scalar cut, both adjacent swaps are always available. Their word determines the labelled path from its initial history. To apply Response 46 with different names, ensure every encoded symbol acts as the identity permutation, and fit the start and finish to the common target permutation of $121$ and $212$. Encode each symbol and each of the two fresh markers by $11\,2^{2i}\,11$ with distinct $i\ge2$. After the entire marked word add the fixed trailer $111222111$. The symbol blocks act trivially on the names and the trailer reverses them. Use $212\to E(LuR)\,111222111$, the encoded production pairs at $D$, and $E(LvR)\,111222111\to121$. Each pair has parallel labelled faces. The trailer contains no alternating triple, and its odd run of twos cannot match a symbol. The block alignment and unique-marker arguments of Response 46 therefore apply at each rewrite. Conversely an aligned rewrite is available at its required history $D$ since every complete preceding block acts trivially. All declarations occupy the three occurrences, and neither an extra generator of the base nor a nonempty edge path appears in an exchange between these histories. The old fixed-hom lifting theorem supplies raw faces at matching old poles; they can be found effectively by enumerating raw writings with the specified strict values. Thus the reduction holds for **each fixed base and chart** in this row, including three distinct names. This theorem concerns one old 4-type while the attachments vary. Unrestricted Q2 also asks about all other old types in a given context.

**There is an all-boundary criterion for Gray conservativity in degree four with braid-preserving 4-attachments.** Let $B$ be any finite Gray 2-computad. Fix any binary surface containing $I$. Then:

1. At every old 4-type $s\to t$, the surface has a filler exactly when $\beta(s)=\beta(t)$.
2. The surface is conservative at **every** old 4-type exactly when each bare spatial triple of 2-generators, with its specified gap paths, has a 4-declaration with the strict reverse cube faces. This is decidable even when the base has infinitely many gap paths.
3. For conservativity *through* degree four, require in addition the elementary square returns of Response 2. On a single scalar, one declaration at the reverse cube therefore raises the first failure to degree five. Take a metrizable locally equiconnected space $W$. This means there is a continuous interpolation $m(x,y,t)$ on a neighbourhood of the diagonal, from $x$ to $y$, constant for $x=y$. For points having overlapping positive supports, interpolate first to their normalized coordinatewise minimum and then to the other point, within the two respective simplices. The usual realization and this metric realization have the same weak type by the nerve lemma on the open vertex stars; each nonempty finite intersection contracts toward the barycentre of the selected vertices in both topologies.

Use the subspace topology in the product with the compact-open path space. Faces are its endpoints, identity has length zero, and top composition concatenates in elapsed time. These formulas are continuous, also at length zero: a normalized family converging to a constant path converges uniformly there, and when the two lengths tend to zero both normalized paths converge to the same constant at the common seam. For $j=1$ the fixed boundary below the endpoints is empty. In general set $B_j=M_{j-1}\times_{B_{j-1}}M_{j-1}$, with $B_0=*$.

The endpoint map $M_j\to B_j$ is a Hurewicz fibration. Given a homotopy of the two endpoints and an initial normalized path, lift the path over their common moving lower boundary using $M_{j-1}\to B_{j-1}$. The initial edge and two end edges of the parameter square are prescribed. Their inclusion is a cofibration and a deformation retract, giving the relative homotopy lift with arbitrary parameter spaces. A length at time $t$ can be taken to be $L+t$, which retains the given path at $t=0$. This also starts the induction at $W\to *$.

Fix once at each rank a continuous choice of endpoint transport for this fibration with the following extra property. If the starting cell is an identity and the two endpoint paths agree, the transported cell is the identity throughout. To construct it let $K$ consist of starting cells and compatible endpoint homotopies $(u(t),v(t))$. The indicated identity data make a closed subspace $K_0$. Each $M_i$ inherits a local interpolation by interpolating lengths linearly and normalized paths pointwise using the lower interpolation; corresponding globular faces interpolate by that same rule. In particular an interpolated length zero has constant normalized path, and fixed lower boundaries stay fixed. Near $K_0$ shrink the initial normalized path pointwise to its start $u(0)$ by this interpolation, shrink its length linearly to zero, and move $v(t)$ to $u(t)$ by the same interpolation. Forgetting just the *outermost* Moore length gives a map
$$ d_j:G_j\longrightarrow D_jG. $$
This map is relatively **trivially fibrant** in (15). Before $R$, a boundary lift over a simplex of normalized paths only needs an outer length: extend the given nonnegative length and make it positive off the simplex boundary, with length one possible if there is no boundary. At its zeroes the prescribed normalized path is constant. The same proof applies to fixed points since the action does not change length. Now $R$ commutes with the fixed-boundary path construction, which is a finite limit using powers by the interval. Apply (15) to this objectwise trivial fibration. These arguments use Kan lifting on singular complexes; the ordinary Moore boundary fibration itself uses only the square lift and the positive extension of length in Response 57.

Hereafter take singular complexes. Adjoin the smaller constraint subcomplexes as above and lift over the selected track and its previously specified matching lifts. For both choices the input limits and imposed loci restrict correctly on constraint intersections. Work on one permutation orbit of indices at a time. A rank-$k$ head now has an action on $G$. For the first $k-1$ stages of its tuple sweep, transport the initial identity along the two lower evaluated face tracks by the first choice. If $g=1$, it is trivial exactly when it is cyclic. A surface decision at the displayed fixed boundary would therefore decide triviality. This reduction applies even with the promise $g=1$. Its other edges give free generators, and the only remaining relations are the orders of the retained cyclic generators. has a concrete image. At every graph the members of $I$ are consecutive in its order and have identical signed edge labels to each outside vertex (read each edge from inside towards that vertex). This identifies the product of posets with the full subposet of those graphs. Its two inverse projections restrict to one representative of $I$ together with the outside names, and to $I$ itself. This describes its realized image and inverses as well. Inflation by a fixed $y\in W(I)$ means substituting $y$ at the identified name. Apply it pointwise to the graph values at the bottom of a Moore globe, retaining every duration.

At each positive local rank choose transport of a starting globe along a path of its parallel boundary as in Response 59. We require it to preserve all signed pair bounds, to give identity transport for a diagonal boundary starting at an identity, and to commute with inflation by **any stationary $y$**. The latter includes $y$ varying with the external simplex parameter, held fixed in all globe times and in the boundary homotopy parameter. We justify these simultaneous requirements.

Call $I$ stationary in a transport input if throughout its starting globe and boundary paths all graph values are inflated with the same $y$ at that simplex parameter. This condition defines a simplicial subset of the input data. On it the compressed input and $y$ are recovered by the two restrictions above, with $y$ read at the initial configuration. There is an intersection property. For disjoint stationary sets, compression of one retains the other. Two intersecting stationary sets $I,J$ have stationary union, and compression of either retains the image of the union as a stationary set. Indeed at a graph their union is an interval; an external vertex sees the same signed level at every member using any member of the intersection. Within the union, the edge between $i\in I\setminus J$ and $j\in J\setminus I$ is determined by the edge between $i$ and a common member, using the block $J$. These facts also apply to compressed graphs. For realized points, restriction to $I$ and $J$ jointly determines the graph point on their union on this locus. To see this, view a point of a poset nerve as the step function on the unit interval listing its chain in order with the barycentric weights as interval lengths, up to values at subdivision points. A monotone map acts pointwise and coalesces equal entries. Apply the graph argument at each common subdivision. Thus constant restrictions give a constant point on the union, even for a family of nonvertex configurations.

Induct in $|S|$. On each stationary-block input locus for $|I|\ge2$, transport on $S/I$ and inflate the resulting family by its given $y$. Disjoint prescriptions agree by compressing both sets; overlapping ones agree by compressing to their union, using the intersection property and the induction on smaller sets. A change in the representative of a quotient name is covered by equivariance. For imposed pair constraints on $S$, internal constraints are satisfied by $y$. For an edge incident to the compressed name impose the intersection of the corresponding exterior constraints, expressed in the same orientation. The compressed data satisfy these constraints, so their transported inflation does too. The diagonal identity prescription agrees on these loci because inflation preserves zero lengths and faces.

On the remaining transport inputs use the relative cylinder lift of Response 59 for $M_l(W(S;U))\to B_lM(W(S;U))$. The boundary fibration follows by the Moore square lift of Response 57. Prescribe the starting endpoint, the prisms on the stationary-block loci, the diagonal identity prescription, and the prisms from smaller internal constraint subcomplexes. The domain inclusion is the pushout product of the endpoint inclusion with a monomorphism, hence is a trivial cofibration. Intersections of constraint subcomplexes are again among the finite constraints. Fixed simplices for a nontrivial permutation stabilizer are absent since its initial named configuration has a free action. Thus equivariant lifts follow by taking orbits of simplicial horns (equivalently use the fixed-point lifting criterion). This constructs the required transport. It may also be taken constant on constant boundary paths, by prescribing that subcomplex in the same lift. At $S=\varnothing$ the entire action is unique. [Complete graph multiplication](https://math.univ-cotedazur.fr/~cberger/config.pdf#page=6) · [Moore boundary lift](#researcher-response-57) · [Relative cylinder construction](#researcher-response-59)

### A static filler compatible with every standard refinement

In degree $n$ use the block composite of Response 63 for each head. For a static tuple all higher labels at each depth-$n$ position are identities on its configuration $x_a$. On the nonempty positions let $\delta$ be their planar signed divergence graph. Write $W_\delta\subset W(S)$ for its exterior upper bounds and define $b_\delta$ on its graphs by leaving the internal graphs alone and setting every exterior edge to its prescribed divergence. This is a monotone map below the identity. Its natural transformation to the identity induces a canonical homotopy on $W_\delta$, preserving each internal graph *point*, even when that point varies with an external parameter. On any more restricted carrier with bounds within the blocks it stays in those bounds.

Here is the inductive invariant in addition to typing. Inflation of one named occurrence throughout its input position by a stationary nonempty configuration commutes with each operation. Outputs retain the signed bounds within each input position and acquire the exterior bounds of its divergence. These assertions for subexpressions follow by applying them along the named tuple: each strict $n$-source uses at most one member of a transport class, and an exterior separation in a substituted face occurs no earlier and in the same order at equal depth. This is the positional lemma used in Response 63. A subexpression that misses the inflated occurrence uses exactly its original labels. The rank-$n$ block formulas have both properties. Consequently, on a static tuple all bottom graph values of an already interpreted *full face*, at every Moore time, lie in $W_\delta$ and have restriction exactly $x_a$ in each block. For the second assertion compress every nonempty position to a separate singleton and then inflate by its $x_a$. Positions that were empty stay empty in the compressed tuple. Parallel full faces visit the same positions. [Pair bounds and occurrence lifts](#researcher-response-63)

For a head of degree $k=n+l>n$, consider its two evaluated $(l-1)$-faces at the static tuple. Contract them **together** by first applying the homotopy to $b_\delta$ pointwise to every graph value, retaining their Moore durations. They end at globes whose graph values are all the single block composite of the $x_a$. Now scale all durations, at every nested level, by a factor decreasing from one to zero, retaining normalized parameters. At zero take the identity tower on the common configuration. This is continuous for the normalized Moore topology: at positive inner rank the varying clocks converge uniformly to zero on each compact parameter cube and the bottom graph is already constant. Both stages commute with faces, giving a path of parallel boundaries. In reverse it starts at the boundary of the identity tower. Transport that tower along the reversed path by the single transport fixed above. Its output is the static filler at the two specified faces. For empty $S$ take the unique filler.

This construction preserves the stated bounds. For inflation inside one position the graph homotopy is literally the inflation of the old homotopy: both monotone maps in the natural transformation insert the same internal graph and induce the old maps on the compressed sets. This holds on products of realized nerves by naturality of the natural-transformation homotopy, including for nonvertex internal graphs. The clock contraction commutes with inflation and the chosen transport was made to do so. This proves the inflation property of the static step.

Consider a published insertion at this static step. The joined tree refines the old partition of its $n$-positions, retaining the exterior divergences between different old positions. Within the replaced position the new divergences are exactly those of the standard inserted tree. In the root-list splice this just replaces a disc column by its list; below a longer branch the common trunk retains the outside column and the assertion follows in its child. If the insertion is deeper than the $n$-cut, the partition is unchanged. An empty position contributes no pairs. This is the exact divergence formula of Response 35. The standard composite on a static inserted block is the block configuration with its internal splits fixed at these new divergences, identity-padded at higher rank. By lower-rank substitution the two face globes before contraction agree on the two sides. Each of their graph values restricts to this *fixed* internal point on the old replaced block by the inflation property. In particular every graph in its supporting simplex has the prescribed edge on each newly exterior pair inside that block. The coarse $b_\delta$ leaves these edges as they are; the refined $b_\delta$ sets them to those very values. The two maps therefore coincide on the whole common subposet where these edges are fixed. Their natural-transformation homotopies coincide there too. The clock contractions, starting towers, and transports are consequently identical. This proves the required equality for the static filler of an **arbitrary** outer head. [Divergences at tree insertion](#researcher-response-35)

### From static tuples to the full published action

The standard operations above degree $n$ have the following independent formula. In the top degree of a cut use Moore concatenation for a local cut and the graph block operation at degree $n$ for a spatial cut. Lift either serially above its degree, holding later factors at their sources and completed factors at their targets. Equivalently, order the strings in the negative section by planar position as in Response 57, now across all depth-$n$ positions. At stage $j>n$ distribute the elapsed time among the $j$-paths of that entire section, retaining prefixes and filling unused slots by zero-length identities as in that response. Each depth-$n$ subtree is a local Moore tuple, so these instructions give a globular tuple, starting at its initial static tuple and ending at the original one. The total $L_j$ is the sum of the lengths over the entire list. Paths on the empty set contribute zero. Standard evaluation in dimension $j$ follows the lower standard evaluation on the target section during this sweep with duration $L_j$.

The whole-tuple insertion formula (14) holds at every $j>n$. At a root-list splice the replaced disc contributes a consecutive block to the list, and the serial standard path on that block has the sum length and precisely its elapsed prefixes. In a longer branch the single outer column of the inserted tree retains all earlier and later times and gives the child calculation with the elapsed time in that column. At the bottom of this recursion the standard $n$-evaluation commutes with insertion by the exact divergence formula above. Thus the early and late tuples agree after the exterior substitution at every fraction; this includes their initial static tuples. In particular the standard evaluations themselves commute with insertion.

For an arbitrary head start at its static filler. Through stages $n+1,\ldots,k-1$ use transport along the two evaluated face tracks. In the final stage the negative $(k-1)$-section stays fixed, hence so does the source face, by its strict support. Append the evaluated target track, of Moore length $L_k$, at its fixed lower boundary. For arity of smaller height this last track has length zero. The construction preserves bounds by the positional lemma and the choice of transport. It respects nonempty stationary inflations: these keep all clocks, prefixes and parameters, preserve the lower operations by induction, and commute with transport and concatenation. This establishes the invariant for the next rank, including for general moving tuples.

At a standard head the two static faces coincide at the standard identity tower. The early boundary tracks are diagonal since all labels in degree $k$ are still identities, so the early transports are identities. Appending the last track gives exactly the independent standard operation. A disc therefore has its prescribed variable value. At a generic endo the static contraction and the early stages have diagonal boundaries, and the final length is zero by the arity height bound. This gives precisely identity on the evaluated face. In an insertion the static fillers agree by the preceding calculation. The remaining transports and the last track agree by the whole-tuple insertion formula, lower-rank substitution and the equal last lengths. In degree $n$ insertion is the exact divergence formula, and in lower degrees all operations are unique. Equal generic bound types supply the same face functions on the same tree, so all these operations respect head congruence and conversion. This verifies the published rules on the coloured quotient, using the unique occurrence transport along a tuple as in Response 63. [Published rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05303) · [Whole-tuple sweep and final stage](#researcher-response-57)

### Detecting the degree without strict forgetting maps

For one depth-$n$ position, on any static tuple the output in local positive degree is the identity tower on its configuration. Indeed both faces are such towers by induction, and the contraction fixes their point. Thus the local raw action on each $M_\bullet(W(S))$ agrees on constant tuples with the fundamental action. The interpolation and normalization of Response 57 compare the local action to the fundamental raw groupoid of $W(S)$, equivariantly under relabelling. The interpolation uses relative simplicial cylinder lifts as in Response 59 for the actions on singular complexes. The comparison identifies the sphere formed by a pair of parallel globes with their two normalized disks glued along their boundary: in the interpolating path action take the constant external paths on the two globes, then normalize the clocks. This observation applies also to the local comparison of Response 63, followed by evaluation of its cone at the full-set vertex.

Send the raw scalar generators to their singleton configurations. For each set of distinct names we have a diagram in groupoidal fixed homs from the binary model of Response 63 back along its raw weak equivalence to the raw skeleton and forward to the new published model. On homotopy types this gives a self-map $F_S$ of $W(S)$ in the equivariant homotopy theory for the permutation action. Let $e$ be its integral degree on two names. We claim $F_S$ multiplies $H_{n-1}$ by $e$ **without** assuming it commutes with erasure.

Take a pair of parallel raw globes representing a generating $(n-1)$-sphere in the ordered two-name component, oriented using the binary comparison. These exist by the fixed-hom globe comparison and the equivalence in Response 63. For any designated pair of names in $S$, place its two globes as the sole moving operand in binary composites at cut $n-1$ with the other, singleton, $n$-cells in fixed slots. Use the same placements for both globes. This is a pair of parallel raw globes, so determines an integral spherical class. In the binary model its normalized disks at the full-set vertex are obtained by the graph block inclusion of the original disks. This follows directly from serial composition with stationary singleton configurations: only the moving operand contributes time in each positive rank. In the published model the independent standard formula gives that same block inclusion of its pair disks. In the complete graph space the projection to the designated pair is the original moving graph and the projection to every other pair is a fixed graph. Since the pair projections are a joint integral coordinate system on $H_{n-1}$, the binary images of these raw spheres are the coordinate basis, and their published images are $e$ times that basis. This proves the claim, also for different orders of names by equivariance. [Integral pair coordinates](#researcher-response-47)

By duality and the generation of configuration cohomology by pair classes, a prime dividing $e$ would make $F_p$ zero on all positive-degree fibre cohomology modulo $p$ on $p$ names. Its cyclic homotopy-orbit map acts identically on the base. The first nonzero differential into the bottom row, which exists by finite dimensionality of the free quotient, gives the contradiction of Response 47. Only equivariance at that cardinality is needed in this step. Therefore $e=\pm1$ and all $F_S$ are equivalences by integral cohomology and simple connectivity. Repeated colours descend by the finite covering and unique named-globe lifts as in Response 63; the construction respects relabelling and merging colours. The empty component is terminal. The delooping, nonstandard point boundaries and disjoint-vertex arguments of that response now give the asserted raw weak equivalence on the whole scalar computad. Response 32 yields the two mixed-attachment statements. For the iterated contexts use the named-strand decoration of Response 37 on this published model: on each tagged sector it is the product of the configuration comparison and the given label comparisons, with the very same cuts for published insertion. Unique occurrence lifting again descends to the untagged hom. This supplies the model after every iteration. The arbitrary finite-computad insertion question still requires control of interactions above this range. ∎

## Researcher Response 68

**Equating adjacent crossing squares gives a decision for every degree-four judgment and for simultaneous reflection at each fixed width.** Work over one Gray scalar, without global 3-generators, with the bare cube return and the two width-three declarations $x^2\rightleftarrows y^2$ for adjacent crossings. Add any finite list of directed 4-declarations of any widths. The decision allows arbitrarily many uses of all declarations. For two classes it decides reflection through four in the **whole context**: when all additional declarations preserve permutation, and when some increase and some decrease crossing count, even at different widths and with different permutations. In particular, the cube return and square comparisons alone give reflection through four at all widths, although the square comparisons change the positive braid. The first failure is then in degree five in the context generated through four. [Fitting and signed contexts](#researcher-response-53) · [Higher obstruction](#researcher-response-29)

At width $n\ge2$ write $\ell(p)$ for the inversion number of $p\in S_n$. Modulo the stipulated mutual comparisons, the positive monoid consists of the pairs $(p,k)$ with $k\ge\ell(p)$ and $k\equiv\ell(p)\pmod2$. Multiplication composes permutations and adds counts. Indeed all adjacent crossing squares equal a common $z$, which commutes with every letter because it is the square of that letter. To reduce a word, peel a square into this central factor whenever the next letter shortens the permutation of the preceding reduced word. The prefix can be given a reduced spelling ending in that letter by the braid moves for reduced expressions. Thus the normal form is $z^{(k-\ell(p))/2}s(p)$, where $s(p)$ is any reduced expression. Permutation and count prove uniqueness. In the signed group the same description holds with arbitrary integral $k$ of the prescribed parity, since inverting $z$ already inverts every letter. This embeds the positive monoid in the group. Widths zero and one have only empty crossing words. [Matsumoto's theorem, Theorem 2.1](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/forum-of-mathematics-sigma/article/benderknuth-billiards-in-coxeter-groups/C9E0C21EE951054EBC573222C166C9A3)

Use the counter $h=(k-\ell(p))/2$. For each placement of a rule $(p,L)\to(q,R)$ and each pair of context permutations $u,v$, set $i=upv$, $j=uqv$, $m=\ell(u)+L+\ell(v)$ and
$$
 a=(m-\ell(i))/2,\qquad b=(m+R-L-\ell(j))/2 .
$$
This supplies exactly $(i,a+t)\to(j,b+t)$ for every $t\ge0$ raw, or every $t\in\mathbb Z$ on the surface. Indeed reduced contexts attain the two thresholds together, and every other possible total context count differs by an even amount. This accounts for arbitrary positive and signed contexts by Response 53. Raw reachability is therefore one-counter reachability with finite control. For signed reachability each move multiplies the current permutation on the left by $u q p^{-1}u^{-1}$ and adds $R-L$ to the total count. With all costs of one weak sign, search between the endpoint counts. With both signs, taking each multiplier to its permutation order gives pure integral translations of both signs. Their nonnegative combinations contain both directions of their gcd $P>0$ by Bézout and opposite signs. Finite search on $S_n\times\mathbb Z/P$ is exact since every discrepancy of a lifted path is a multiple of $P$. [Balanced one-counter decision](#researcher-response-49)

**Testing all old boundaries at once.** For each compiled transition with $e=b-a$, require the raw comparison $(i,\max(0,-e))\to(j,\max(0,e))$. Put $C=\max |e|$ (zero for no transitions). For every pair of controls and both endpoint heights in $[0,C)$, test that signed reachability implies raw reachability. All tests are necessary. For sufficiency, split a signed path at every nonnegative configuration. A single edge between nonnegative configurations is a positive translate of its first test. An excursion strictly below zero starts and ends at heights less than $C$, so its whole comparison is supplied by the second tests. Concatenation gives a raw path. A failed test directly specifies two old positive words by the normal form. For example, adjoining $x^3\to y^3$ yields a surface comparison $x\to y$ at width three by cancelling $z$. There is no raw use of this rule at count one, and the two permutations differ.

**Two finite tests over unbounded widths.** If all additional rules preserve permutation, each signed move translates height by its cost $d=(R-L)/2$. At the rule's own width require the raw comparison $z^{\max(0,-d)}\to z^{\max(0,d)}$. It is necessary by signed translation. Its stationary paddings supply the same comparison at every larger width. Concatenation with $s(i)$ and powers of $z$ supplies it at every allowed positive height for every control. For a signed path between positive endpoints, perform its increases first and then its decreases. This gives sufficiency simultaneously, without any bound on widths or number of uses.

If both signs of count change occur, let $N$ be the first width where both occur. First test simultaneous reflection at each width below $N$. At $N$ choose one available rule of each strict sign. For each, multiply its absolute count change by the order of its permutation defect $qp^{-1}$. The lcm of the two positive products is $2H$ with $H>0$ (a pure count translation has even count). The signed order at $N$ has $1\rightleftarrows z^H$ by repetition. Test just these two raw judgments at $N$. A failure witnesses nonreflection. On success their stationary paddings give $z^H$ mutually comparable with the identity at every larger width. In the positive monoid modulo mutual raw comparison this makes each crossing a unit, since its $2H$-th power is the identity. Every signed context thus acts by a positive representative, also for declarations first available above $N$, proving sufficiency. For instance $1\rightleftarrows xy$ at width three gives $1\rightleftarrows(xy)^3=z^3$. With the stipulated square comparisons and cube return, **arbitrary further rules of width at least three** then preserve reflection through four. The mechanism can first occur above width two. ## Researcher Response 69

**Single-crossing insertion reflects at every width once adjacent squares are mutually comparable.** In the one-scalar context of Response 68 adjoin the width-two insertion $1\to x$. For old faces represented by positive words of counts $k,K$ and permutations $p,q\in S_n$, both raw and surface inhabitation in degree four are equivalent to
$$
             K-k\ \ge\ n-\#\mathrm{cycles}(p^{-1}q).
$$
Count fixed points as cycles. On success there is an explicit raw certificate with exactly $K-k$ individual insertions. In particular the four-strand pair of Response 54 now has a two-insertion raw witness. The square declarations change the surface preorder as well. The formula still decides both judgments after adjoining any directed rules whose count increase is at least the transposition distance between their two permutations. [Positive and signed normal forms](#researcher-response-68) · [Four-strand insertion boundary](#researcher-response-54)

In the signed group a contextual insertion acts by any conjugate transposition with count cost one. The least number of transpositions taking $p$ to $q$ is the displayed cycle deficit $d$: multiplying by a transposition splits or joins two cycles, and a cycle of length $m$ can be split with $m-1$ transpositions. Parity of the face counts forces $K-k-d$ even, and repeating a transposition twice spends any even excess. This proves signed necessity and sufficiency. Stationary padding preserves both cost and distance, so additional rules as above already belong to this order.

For the raw construction insert the even excess in pairs of identical letters at the start, without changing its permutation. It remains to travel distance $d$ between positive endpoints with count gap exactly $d$. Whenever $p\ne q$, take a nontrivial cycle of $p^{-1}q$ on the positions. The two lists of values of $p$ and $q$ on these positions have the same underlying set. At least one list has an inverted pair, since otherwise their increasing lists coincide positionwise. Swap the positions of an inverted pair on an endpoint where it occurs. This strictly reduces inversion number there and splits the relative cycle, decreasing $d$ by one. Either endpoint can be used. The following two constructions explain why the step has the correct positive orientation in both cases.

* At the source take a reduced spelling $A x B$ of $p$ in which the crossing of the two inverted strands is designated. In every reduced spelling they cross once: each step adds exactly one inversion. Skipping that crossing swaps the two terminal positions' values, so $AB$ represents the chosen lower permutation. Insert $x$ beside the designated crossing to get $A x^2 B=z AB$. The new source has count one higher and lower inversion number.
* At the target take the corresponding reduced spelling $A x B$ of $q$ and pass back to $AB$ at count one lower. Its inversion number is at most $|AB|$. A final positive insertion recovers $A x B$. At both endpoints carry along the existing central square factors, which matches the specified counts exactly.

Continue with the smaller distance. At distance zero the two counts coincide and Response 68 identifies the positive words by their permutation and count. Pasting the saved target insertions in reverse order gives the certificate. For any additional rule satisfying the distance bound the construction already gives its raw comparison at its own width, so both orders retain the same formula.

Into that value substitute the $v_i$ restricted to $L_m$; on a Moore globe do this to each bottom graph, retaining all clocks. Chain faces, including the last one, commute by graph restriction. Repeated images use the cone degeneracies. Successive substitutions compose literally since images of subsets compose and the internal and external edges give operad substitution. In particular a moving cell can have a positive outer clock after all its names disappear. The induced $v$ is unique on this locus, read on the full-set configuration restricted to $I$. The transported data have an initial configuration for this test in every rank.

Here is why the prescriptions agree, even on chains that meet only part of a stationary block. For disjoint blocks the two idempotents commute. Fix an old parallel pair of 3-faces and a binary surface containing $I$. A site is an **occurrence** of a vertex along the common underlying edge path (including its ends). Revisiting a vertex gives a different site. There is no bound on the number of visited sites, path cycles, repeated names, signs of changes or widths of the declarations. The solver computes a finitely generated additive monoid of integer vectors and tests a single membership. Three events at one site already permit undecidability by Response 60. Even at multiplicity two the locations must be considered jointly. [Width-three undecidability](#researcher-response-60) · [Single-site named order](#researcher-response-56)

At each site containing two events record the crossing exponent of the face obtained by retaining just those two strands. An exchange between distinct sites contributes zero. Write $D$ for the tuple of target minus source exponents. For each declaration, place its entire edge path as a consecutive subpath of the queried path, matching vertices, and require its scalar multiset at each site to fit in the queried multiset there, with names. For each such placement take the vector of its exponent changes, translated to the queried sites and extended by zeros. The surface type is inhabited exactly when $D$ is a nonnegative integer combination of these vectors. A declaration with more than two events at a site can never fit. Distinct names at a two-event site force even differences between parallel faces there; both incoming orders are accounted for by signed transport.

**Why the coordinates suffice.** A temporal history orders the scalar events. A positive swap of adjacent events is available when the left-listed site is spatially at or to the right of the right-listed site; its signed inverse is available in the surface. Stably sort each history by site using just positive swaps of distinct sites. All such sorting paths compare both ways by the adjacent cube and distant moves: they are reduced expressions of the same sorting permutation, and every reduced expression swaps only the required inversions. An exchange of distinct sites followed by sorting agrees, up to these comparisons, with sorting first; use the reverse statement after cancellation for a negative exchange. A same-site exchange can be carried through the sorting path to the corresponding adjacent pair in the sorted block. Sort its two consecutive events as a single block. Passing a third event across the block commutes with the designated swap by one adjacent braid relation, in the direction supplied by the native cube or its surface return. Disjoint moves commute, and an inverse swap follows by cancellation. All these relations use the actual positions along the path. Once sorted, different sites commute by distant moves. At a site with two events a signed word is an arrow of the named two-strand braid groupoid, determined by its exponent and input names. Thus two signed paths with the same temporal endpoints and local exponents compare both ways, with the weak inverses and fittings of Responses 52–56. For surface sufficiency, whisker a placed rule by the remaining edge paths and append all unused scalar events in a stationary temporal suffix. Signed swaps can take the current initial history to this source because the named site multisets agree. Supply a signed suffix so that the rule's left face with these outer paths represents the current arrow (compose with the inverse of the prefixed left face). The right face then contributes exactly the stipulated vector. Repeat according to the integer coefficients and fit at the final old faces by the sorting comparison. For necessity one must also rule out comparisons arising by conversion at another boundary. Use the following ordered Gray-category in the column-order and history models of Response 5. Its objects and 1-arrows are vertices and paths. At a path its 2-endomorphisms are tuples of named lists, one per site, and its 3-arrows are tuples of named braids. There are no 2-arrows between different paths. In a fixed hom, concatenate lists and juxtapose their braids sitewise, and stack composable braids. Whiskering by a path pads with empty sites. At a composable pair of paths the tensorator is the structural block braid between the incident lists at the joint vertex, and identity elsewhere. This gives the Gray operations: their unit, composition and naturality equations at the joint site are the braided unit, hexagon and naturality equations, and operations on separate sites commute componentwise. For several entirely stationary paths at the same vertex these are precisely the usual doubly degenerate Gray operations of a braided monoidal category.

On profiles with at most two events per site order parallel arrows by the stated vector monoid. On profiles with higher multiplicity allow every comparison. The resulting orders respect all operations. Whiskering and juxtaposition only add events, extend the path, or include a vector with zeros at new coordinates. Two-strand exponents are additive in composite or common context, and a larger multiplicity cannot become smaller by any of these operations. Every declared comparison therefore holds in its own profile. The column-order value of an old exchange is exactly the specified tuple (different sites have identity interchanger), by the generic-head calculation of Response 52. The history model interprets the surface and changes the two old values by common endpoint isomorphisms. Their exponent difference is invariant. This proves necessity without assuming that every surface derivation is initially written in sorted form. [Ordered Gray history construction](#researcher-response-5)

**Exact complexity example.** Every finitely generated submonoid of $\mathbb Z^d$ occurs. Take a path through $d$ different vertices, with two occurrences of the same local scalar at each. Use the entire path and the entire sorted history for each rule. For the vector $v$, take the positive source and target site counts to be its coordinatewise negative and positive parts. Both 3-faces are loops there, and the path has only one placement. For the family in which every rule inserts three single crossings on three distinct sites and the query asks for one at every site, the surface decision is NP-complete in the explicit crossing-list encoding. Columns are exactly triples, and any certificate is a set of disjoint triples covering all the sites. Conversely any exact-cover instance gives this presentation with polynomial size. Conversely read the three same-site crossing counts on any intermediate positive 3-face, whether or not it has the specified spelling. **Finite tests for every old pair at these temporal endpoints.** Let $M$ be the surface vector monoid from Response 74, including placements in *other* temporal orders. This positive monoid has effectively finitely many nonzero indecomposables. **At any old degree-four boundary over a finite Gray 2-computad, arbitrary directed 4-attachments reduce to one finite group presentation with a finite list of directed defects.** There are no global 3-generators. There is also a direct, exact test for the group to be trivial before any 4-attachments: the finite positive exchange graph in the query's signed component must be acyclic. In that case all old parallel positive paths in the component compare on the surface, and raw comparison is decidable for arbitrary 4-attachments.

**The finite presentation.** Start at the strict temporal source history of the query. A vertex records the ordered sequence of rewrite names with their positions in the evolving edge path. Add a positive edge for each legal adjacent exchange of the spatially right event past the left one; explore in both directions, retaining the original oriented edge, including loops and parallel edges. The inverse removes that same exchange with the position adjusted by the length change of the left rewrite. This search is finite: it preserves the initial edge path and multiset of events, and no intermediate edge word has length greater than the initial length plus the sum of the positive event length changes. Attach a square for every distant swap pair and a hexagon for each executable braid relation of three adjacent events. These are the actual contextual cubes at those positions, including their edge gaps. Contract a spanning tree. The remaining oriented edges and face boundaries give an ordinary finite group presentation $G$. A signed path now spells a group word by ignoring tree edges.

Also enumerate each declared face pair at every vertex, consecutive temporal interval and spatial subpath placement where its initial history agrees. Compare the spatial subpath against the edge word **after the preceding temporal prefix**; the full rule and any remaining temporal events are then well typed. Add $r l^{-1}$ to the directed list, where $l,r$ are its placed paths after tree contraction. For query paths $u,v$ the target is $v u^{-1}$. Contraction of the tree identifies the connected path groupoid with this group at fixed endpoints. Composable signed outer paths give all conjugates of each defect: a prefix transports to the rule, and its suffix can be chosen to give any specified current left-side arrow. Hence products of conjugates are precisely chains of contextual moves.

**Soundness for arbitrary surface conversion.** Form a usual Gray-category with vertices, edge paths and temporal rewrite histories of the base in dimensions zero to two. Its 3-arrows are signed exchange paths between histories, modulo the squares and hexagons above. In a fixed hom, composition concatenates temporal histories, with 3-paths pasted in the two blocks; the distant squares give the strict functor law. Spatial 1-path whiskering pads the edge paths. The tensorator of two spatially separated temporal histories is their block exchange, moving one entire list past the other by elementary positive swaps. Successive block exchanges satisfy the unit and composition axioms: the two orders that move a rectangular block of swaps differ by commutations of independent swaps. Naturality with an elementary exchange **inside** a moving block follows by passing it across one opposite event at a time. Each passage uses one three-event hexagon, with distant swaps for the unaffected positions. The inverse elementary exchange follows by cancellation, and composition gives naturality for all signed paths. This constructs the required Gray-category with invertible tensorators without identifying parallel signed paths merely because they forget to the same permutation.

Order the parallel 3-arrows by the placed declarations with signed outer paths. This family is preserved by the Gray operations. With the generating assignment, the raw column operation reads the actual positive exchange path: the generic-head comparison takes a directed interchanger to this model's tensorator, before specializing the labels.
