Here $QK$ is the simplicial bar resolution of a diagram $K$: in bar dimension $d$ use a copy of $K(i_0)\times y_{i_d}$ for each chain $i_0\to\cdots\to i_d$, then realize. At an index its augmentation to $K$ is an equivalence by the terminal-arrow extra degeneracy. Filtering by nondegenerate chains shows that $Q$ takes monomorphisms to projective cofibrations, hence also takes objectwise trivial monomorphisms to projective trivial cofibrations. By the tensor adjunction $\operatorname{Map}(K,RA)=\operatorname{Map}(QK,A)$, $R$ takes objectwise Kan fibrations and trivial fibrations to injective ones. For objectwise Kan $A$, $A\to RA$ is an objectwise equivalence, since $Qy_i\to y_i$ is an equivalence between projectively cofibrant diagrams. $R$ commutes with limits and interval powers. Its coordinates are compatible functions on simplices of strings of outgoing arrows, with the terminal value in the hom at the image pair. In particular composition and the tuple operations involving more than one hom can be applied at the *same string and parameter* in each input, because the outgoing index arrows are the same for all the input pairs.

Use as local $(l+1)$-cells on $a,b$ the vertices of $G_l=R\operatorname{Sing} M_l W$, with the Moore globes of Response 57, $M_0 W=W$. The local arrows compose by enriched composition pointwise. Above them the serial standard operations, tuple sweeps and top concatenation also act pointwise. They are natural for continuous maps with their clocks retained. For $l\ge1$ both lift maps required in Response 59 are available as *diagram* maps: the globe boundary projection is an injective fibration and forgetting the outer length to a normalized track is an injective trivial fibration. Before $R$ these are objectwise fibrations by the boundary prism lift and the positive length extension (relative to the prescribed lengths), respectively. The boundary limits and normalized track powers commute with $R$. For transport, attach the endpoint cylinder relative to the subcomplex on which the starting cell is an identity and the boundary paths agree. This is an objectwise trivial monomorphism. For the normalized track lift use the monomorphism given by the two prescriptions $q(a,d a)=a$ and $q(1,c)=1_v$ for $c$ constant at $v$. The prescriptions agree on their intersection. Injective lifting gives the two operations simultaneously at all indices, including relabellings and every arrow from a pure cut. For inputs with intermediate objects, the tuple diagram over an outside pair takes the disjoint union over the intermediate objects.

Now use the directed construction of Response 57 starting at the tuple of initial arrows in the columns, with their strict composite as the initial value. From local degree two onwards use its serial sweeps, transporting the identity along the earlier boundary tracks and appending $q$ of the standard reference and the actual final track. Standard evaluation and the entire tuple sweep obey (14) on each bar coordinate. On a standard head transport is diagonal and $q$ gives the reference; on an endo it gives the identity. At an insertion the lower boundary tracks, reference and final track coincide on the two evaluations by (14). These are the checks of Responses 57 and 59, with the first composition now in $E$. They give published-algebra homomorphisms on all diagram arrows.

The raw reduct presents $E_i$ with the same objects. In detail the normalized fixed-interval globes on its simplicial homs $R\operatorname{Sing}W$ have the usual raw action, using the fixed pasting-ball maps and pointwise exterior composition. These homs are objectwise equivalent to $E_i(a,b)$, naturally with composition. Normalization from $G_l$ to the fixed-interval globes is a trivial fibration relative to globe boundaries by the iterated prism and length lifts, then $R$. Lift the raw action relative to tuples of initial arrows extended by identities. Interpolate this lift and the raw reduct of the published action as in Response 57. In each prescribed object sequence the section of initial-arrow tuples is an objectwise monomorphic equivalence, by the directed tuple sweeps which fix that section. Its cylinder together with the two whole ends therefore includes by a trivial cofibration, and the globe-boundary fibrations above lift the interpolation. Both evaluations of the raw path algebra lift globes at given faces by the one-end prism lift. This gives the natural raw comparison, including the pure groupoids and the characteristic arrows in local degree one. [Directed Moore model and raw comparison](#researcher-response-57) · [Normalized track lifts](#researcher-response-59)

At a split the $G_l$ on any given pair map equivalently to their proper-subset matching limit. Indeed each $M_l W$ is naturally equivalent to $W$ by constant globes, and the derived matching limit of the homs at that pair is the matching hom of $E$, up to equivalence. This follows either by taking mapping spaces in the limit of categories or by the Bergner matching fibrations at the restricted pairs. The representable-union argument applies to pair indices also, since the image of a pair under any restriction is determined. Thus the injective fibrations for $G_l$ compute the derived matching limits and give fibrations *relative to globular boundary* there. Inducting on the boundary rank makes these latter fibrations trivial at a split (start with $G_0$ on a pair). Together with the object lift in $E$ this gives an actual cell at every prescribed matching globe.

Interpret the published fixed hom by the split symbols, grouped local heads and bare variables of Response 86. Its parsing proof uses the trunk threshold at the fixed-hom depth, so applies with $n$ in place of three: an unoccupied subtree has weight zero, a single occupied slot desuspends, and the trunk of a split symbol has height less than $n$. Bounds on signed divergences pass to faces, deletion and normalization by the same positional argument at these $n$ levels. At pure objects use the characteristic graph vertices. Choose pure split lifts equivariantly (a stabilizer fixing the fully named symbol fixes its names), by cardinality then local degree. Use their images under the pure-to-cut arrows for all pure terms at a directed cut. At bare rules use the characteristic arrows with constant bar data. Their restrictions are the characteristic arrows or the identity, and their endpoint graphs are the ordered port graphs. Lift the other split symbols in their own constrained interval relative to their already interpreted proper restrictions and faces. Evaluate grouped heads by the diagram's published action. This gives the local published map and hence, on the raw category, a functor
$$
                               F:C\longrightarrow C
$$
up to the raw comparison just constructed. Each object is at its own cut, so this is a functor over the cut poset: a functor to a poset is determined by its object values. Restriction to the pure stratum is a weak equivalence. Indeed on the pure indices we have untruncated maps of ordered configuration spaces coherent for all partial bijections. On pair classes they multiply by one common degree $e$. For any prime dividing $e$ the positive cohomology rows of the cyclic $p$-name Borel spectral sequence map to zero mod $p$, while the base row map is the identity. Freeness and finite dimensionality force a first nonzero differential to the base row, a contradiction. Thus $e=\pm1$. Pair classes generate integral cohomology and the spaces are simply connected of finite CW type. The pure-to-directed index arrow identifies this same equivalence at each cut. A published filler therefore gives a raw filler *after applying $F$*. It remains to prove that $F$ detects the old faces. [Pure degree and diagram comparison](#researcher-response-47) · [Normalized symbols and port observations](#researcher-response-86)

### Factoring a computation through intermediate cuts

For $I<J$ let $E(I,J)$ now denote the **space of arrows with both endpoints varying** over $X_I\times X_J$ in $C$. Its homotopy fibre is the fixed-end arrow space. For a chain of intermediate cuts take the space of strings through those cuts, also with all configurations varying. Intrinsically these are the cores of the corresponding functor categories $\operatorname{Fun}([d],C)$ with fixed cut sequence. By the Segal property they are homotopy fibre products of the consecutive arrow spaces over the intermediate strata. Let $L(I,J)$ be the homotopy colimit over nonempty chains of strictly intermediate cuts, with maps composing at omitted cuts. Composition gives $L(I,J)\to E(I,J)$. This construction is functorial over the cut poset, in particular for $F$.

In the schedule model a string through a chain is the homotopy colimit over schedules retaining those cuts. To see this, take the schedule formulas on each consecutive interval and compose by the homotopy coend over each intermediate configuration groupoid. The two paths to the varying intermediate point concatenate to the one intervening path in (16), by the representable coend. Composition of several such identifications is the same multi-coend. Equivalently use the products of permutohedra in the enriched cubical resolution of Response 82, where composition is exactly the ordered-face inclusion. Consequently $L\to E$ is modeled by the subcomplex of schedules with an intermediate cut, with their coefficients. In the simplicial replacement every refinement chain in this subcomplex is counted over the nonempty subsets of the interior cuts of its coarsest member. That poset has contractible nerve, giving the asserted equivalence from the homotopy union of the factorization spaces.

If there is dependence among the $k$ events between $I,J$, all schedules have an intermediate cut. Then $L\to E$ is an equivalence. Otherwise the sole additional schedule is the single batch of all $k$ events. Let $Z$ be the configuration of its event sites and stationary wires, and $P$ the $(k-1)$-dimensional permutohedron. The pair $(E,L)$, using a mapping cylinder for a pair when necessary, is obtained from $L$ by attaching $Z'\times P$ along $Z'\times\partial P$. Here $Z'$ consists of a site configuration and the two pure paths to the *varying* ends. Projection $Z'\to Z$ is an equivalence by contraction of the endpoint paths. On this piece source evaluation is homotopic to the input-block expansion $a:Z\to X_I$. Thus
$$
 H^{d+k-1}(E,L;\mathbb Z)\cong H^d(Z;\mathbb Z).
$$
The class corresponding to one is pulled back from the same pair for the bare Boolean cut poset. Indeed setting all configuration coefficients to a point leaves exactly $(P,\partial P)$ relative to the factorable schedules. This also covers a single event, with $L$ empty. The relative cohomology is generated as a module over $H^*(X_I)$ by this one class: on the attaching piece the module action is $a^*$, which is onto since choosing a representative input per site retracts $a$ up to unary homotopy. These assertions use relative excision, including the cap pairing of $H_d(Z)$ with the restrictions of $H^d(X_I)$. [Cubical resolution and site bimodules](#researcher-response-82)

Induct on interval length. The strata are already equivalences. On $L$ the inductive equivalences for proper intervals and strata give an equivalence by the string formula. In the dependent case this proves the claim for $E$. In the independent case $F$ fixes the relative class from the bare poset and induces an automorphism on $H^*(X_I)$. Hence it surjects onto each relative cohomology group, and is an isomorphism there because those groups are finitely generated abelian. The relative homology groups are free of finite rank, by the ordered configuration calculation, so the induced relative homology map is an isomorphism as well. The pair sequence now gives an ordinary homology equivalence on $E$. For $n\ge4$ the strata and the fixed-end homs are simply connected by Response 82, hence so is $E$. Homological Whitehead proves the inductive equivalence in this rank.

### Keeping the attaching class in the universal cover at rank three

We supply the extra information needed when $n=3$. For an independent interval put each event with its ports in its own spatial block and put each stationary wire in its own block. Order the blocks at the last spatial cut. Require their fixed signed exterior divergence throughout, with unrestricted internal graphs. Write $(E_U,L_U)$ for the corresponding factorization pair in that constraint. Its map to the bare Boolean pair is an equivalence on both entries. In fact the constrained category decomposes up to equivalence into the individual block categories by the split product. The space of arrows with varying ends for a single block use is equivalent to its one-site space, which is contractible. For a stationary singleton its configuration is contractible as well. In a cut string the idle steps in each factor are paths in the same pure groupoid; the varying endpoints on those steps contract away by composition. Thus every full string space there is contractible, giving also the assertion on $L_U$. The map of pairs to $(E,L)$ sends the top relative generator to the class of a point of $Z'$ times $[P,\partial P]$. This follows by the same attaching-piece description, since the constrained simultaneous coefficient is nonempty and connected.

Here one needs control of the image of an actual comparison cube under $F$, in addition to its augmentation in ordinary homology. Use the free raw arity given by $n-1$ suspensions of a line of columns, a single 2-globe at each event and a single edge at each stationary wire. Its outside $n$-fold hom presents the Boolean cube. Indeed raw-to-strict on the globular arity lifts at prescribed boundaries, and the indicated strict hom is the cartesian product of the one-arrow categories. Label its column source and target by the ordered input and output composites and its 2-globe by the rule. This gives a functor from the cube to $C$ over cuts. In the raw configuration model it is the ordered block composition of the one-event arrows, hence factors up to equivalence through the constrained category just used. More explicitly, composition along the line of columns is the composition functor on the product of its consecutive homs (the Segal map at the intervening vertices is an equivalence). Its specialization in the iterated point hom is the corresponding ordered little-disks multiplication on those factors. This is part of the free $E_n$-category identification with its generating arrows. In the complete graph model choose the last-level ordered block vertex for this multiplication. Substitution at that vertex inserts the internal configurations pointwise, including on each cube of uses, with exactly the prescribed exterior edges. Choices of the multiplication point in that ordered one-dimensional operation are connected. This describes the whole specialized functor, including its composition comparisons. [Free configuration algebra on the attaching arrows](#researcher-response-78)

The composite of the same raw arity map with $F$ also factors through the constrained category. For clarity, this follows on syntax before passing to the represented cube. At the first $n-1$ spatial levels, any two occupied consecutive factors of a generic argument would each traverse the two distinct poles of the corresponding suspension, which is impossible at their common seam. Thus the occupied part stays in one slot up to the last level. At the last spatial level the strict sources of the occupied slots are consecutive nonempty subpaths of the line of columns, in its order. These statements apply recursively to the labels in each slot, using their own subpath and the same distinct suspension poles whenever the label traverses a column. It follows that marks belonging to different columns can separate only at that last level and in the prescribed order. This is a check on the generic arity: after substitution, a variable contributes only the configurations or use internal to its own column. A split occurring inside a substituted label is accounted for by that label; elsewhere it is the divergence of the distinct occupied slots just computed. Face selection, disc, endo and insertion preserve the indicated bounds by the positional check of Response 86. Consequently all the specialized normal expressions in this fixed hom are evaluated by the published interpretation inside $U$. This gives the factorization even for cells comparing several orders at once. It gives the through-cut factorizations there too, by applying the same argument to every segment of the string. Both maps of the test cube, before and after applying $F$, project to the identity on Boolean cuts.

When $k=1$, $E\simeq Z$ is simply connected. When $k=2$, $L$ has two connected components, one for each order. In the attachment above $Z'$ is simply connected. Van Kampen therefore gives the free product of the two component fundamental groups, with their basepoints connected by one bridge through the attaching cylinder. We can take that bridge from the test cube. Indeed $E_U$ and the corresponding two components of $L_U$ are contractible; the bridge agrees up to paths in those components with the cylinder path at a fixed separated site configuration. After $F$ the bridge still lies in that same constrained pair up to the pair comparison, with the ends in the same respective components. Connect the two new ends to the two original ends inside the respective $L_U$ components. The resulting bridge is homotopic to the original by contractibility of $E_U$. With these basepoint changes $F$ induces the free product of the two component isomorphisms on $\pi_1$, hence an isomorphism. This check matters because an arbitrary path between the two components can conjugate the two factors differently.

For $k\ge3$ in an independent interval the attachment has relative cells only in dimensions at least two, so $\pi_1 L\to\pi_1 E$ is onto ($L$ is connected). Since $F$ is an equivalence on $L$, it is surjective on $\pi_1 E$. This group is Hopfian. Indeed the fixed-end group for an antichain is the finite-graph right-angled Artin group of Response 90. The endpoint fibration over $X_I\times X_J$ quotients this group by the two exterior cut lattices: the connecting map on $\pi_2$ varies just the initial or final pure path, giving precisely the corresponding cut generator. Both lattices in the single-stage basis of Response 90 are generated by subsets of universal vertices. Their union generates a coordinate central summand. The quotient is again a finite-graph right-angled Artin group. Such groups are residually finite (the integral Magnus embedding separates a nonzero coefficient by truncation and reduction modulo an integer), and finite generation makes a residually finite group Hopfian. For the last implication a surjective endomorphism injects, hence permutes, the finite set of maps to each finite group. An element in its kernel therefore vanishes in every finite quotient. This proves the isomorphism on $\pi_1 E$. [The antichain basis](#researcher-response-90) · [Magnus embedding, Wade §4](https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/44295)

Finally pull the pair back to the universal cover of $E$. Relative homology there is one copy of $H_{*-(k-1)}(Z)$ for every deck element, since $Z'\times P$ is simply connected. Choose one lifted bottom generator. The test cube represents such a single generator, up to sign and deck translation: in the constrained model its domain total space is contractible, its map over the bare relative orientation has degree one, and inclusion of the constrained attaching piece picks one point in one lifted $Z'$. The same holds of its image under $F$ by the second constrained factorization. Consequently the lifted $F$ sends the bottom copies bijectively to single bottom copies, using the isomorphism on the deck group. In higher relative degrees it sends each copy to that same copy. To see this, cap the image of a class in one copy with the pullback of any source-stratum cohomology class on the target. By naturality this is the map on bottom copies applied to the cap product with $F^*$ of the stratum class. Hence all evaluations on other copies vanish. The restrictions from $X_I$ pair perfectly in the sense of separating all elements of each $H_d(Z)$, by surjectivity of $a^*$ and freeness. On the surviving copy projection to ordinary relative homology is the identity identification with $H_d(Z)$, where the map was proved an isomorphism. Thus the entire lifted relative map is a homology isomorphism. The lifted map on the preimage of $L$ is an equivalence by induction on its string description and pullback of the covering along the equivalence on $L$ (the covering classified using $F$ is the same up to its deck isomorphism). The lifted pair sequence and simply connected Whitehead now give an equivalence on universal covers and hence on $E$. This completes the interval induction also at rank three.

For every named boundary the endpoint strata and total arrow space have now been compared by equivalences, so taking the homotopy fibre gives an equivalence on the *specified* raw hom. A surface filler interpreted above therefore forces the old difference sphere to vanish there. The fixed-hom globe test gives a raw filler at the old faces, and folding the supported lift returns it in the original finite context. At the lower degrees the strict history and connected-configuration lifts are already Response 82. This proves the claimed all-dimensional result for positive rules, including the first unstable comparisons. Arbitrary higher attaching declarations and the unrestricted Q1–Q2 classifications remain open. ∎

The relative calculation over two prime fields found one top class on each of the 936 Boolean intervals and zero relative groups on every dependent interval. It verified 54 signed port sections and 16,640 factorizations and intersections of partial name maps. On a three-sheet cover of the two-event square, a bridge with an excursion had lifted coefficients $(1,-1,1)$ over one sheet despite augmented degree one. This checks the distinction used in the fundamental-group argument. At ranks three, four and five Rice's checker accepted a raw cell across the full three-use hexagon with two-input, two-output rules, in both raw and SUA modes. Both modes rejected substituting a distinct parallel rule on the same boundary. These checks exercise the relative computation and the spatial cube at literal types; the diagram lifts and universal-cover comparison are proved above. ## Researcher Response 100

**There is an exact graph test for reproducing all old Gray interchange judgments by a finite raw extension with the same 2-skeleton.** Let $B$ be a finite 2-computad with no higher declarations, and fix any binary surface containing $I$. The raw extension may add generators in arbitrary degrees at least three. The requirement is equality of inhabitation at every old type *over $B$*, in every dimension. A finite such extension exists exactly when both conditions hold:

1. For each ordered pair of 2-generators, there are only finitely many stationary edge paths from the terminal object of the first to the initial object of the second.
2. No 2-generator is repeatable: there is no stationary edge path from its terminal object back to its initial object, including the empty path.

If these hold, let $r$ be the maximum length of a spatially composable string of 2-generators. For $r\le1$ no auxiliary declarations are needed. For $r\ge2$ the **least possible ceiling on auxiliary declaration degree is exactly $r+1$**. There is a further nonuniform conclusion: for *any fixed* ceiling on the degrees of the old questions, $d\ge3$, condition 1 alone is necessary and sufficient for a finite realization through $d$. Thus, at the point with a scalar and no edges, every bounded fragment has a finite raw realization although no single finite one works in all dimensions.

**Construction.** For each bare spatial string of $k\ge2$ rewrites with specified middle paths take its native local $k$-cube at its descending temporal source, with no exterior stationary paths. Choose a raw writing of its native global $(k+1)$-cell using the fixed-hom lifting of Response 8. In an initially unbounded extension make each of these cells a coinductive equivalence. Explicitly, at an arrow $F:s\to t$ adjoin two backward arrows and a higher cell from each of the two appropriate cancellation composites to the identity at its pole. Apply the same prescription to those two higher cells and iterate. All expressions use ordinary fixed-hom composition and identities at their written boundaries. Boundary lifts for the original cube can be found by spelling its labelled strict chart and enumerating its raw lifts, whose existence is guaranteed at the arity. The new declarations at each stage then have directly specified raw types. Contextual native cubes are obtained by whiskering, so their images in this extension are equivalences as well.

Write $Y$ for the resulting raw extension. The map from each raw fixed hom of $B$ to that of $Y$ now factors through $L_1A$, the localized hom calculated in Response 98, by the same core and atom argument. In particular $Y$ fills every old boundary in global degree at least five. At degree four, positive braid equality can be realized by either direction of each contextual cube and distant commutations, with fitting at the two old faces. At degree three, inverse squares realize every step of the undirected exchange relation. These are exactly the surface positives by Responses 2 and 52, including the lower-degree agreement. Conversely every added generator is interpretable over $B$ in its chosen surface. Its bare cube is a surface equivalence by Response 98, so choose two inverses and the two equivalence witnesses, then continue recursively at those witnesses. The resulting substitution sends every raw filler in $Y$ at an old type to a surface filler at that type. Thus the comparison gives both directions, including through higher conversion on the surface. [Surface localization of the bare cubes](#researcher-response-98) · [Degree-four braid criterion](#researcher-response-52) · [Degree-three test](#researcher-response-2)

Under condition 1 there are finitely many bare charts of any *bounded* rank, since each successive pair has a finite choice of middle paths. Truncate the displayed construction after global degree $d$, omitting higher cubes and higher inverse witnesses. Only finitely many declarations remain. Every raw term of degree at most $d$ over $Y$ uses only these declarations: the strict support of a full Gray head bounds the degrees of its variables by the degree of its value, and substitutions preserve this dimension bound. Thus the truncation retains all the required raw inhabitants through $d$. Condition 1 is necessary even here, by the long-gap two-event old boundary of Response 81 for any sound fixed-2-skeleton extension. [Degree bound for raw terms](#researcher-response-13) · [Infinite stationary-gap obstruction](#researcher-response-81)

If condition 2 fails, choose repetitions of a repeatable generator of length $k\ge3$ with $k+1$ above the declaration bound of any proposed finite extension. The cube reverse is an old type over $B$, with a surface filler already there, and Response 29 excludes its raw filler even after the lower declarations. This proves all-dimensional necessity. If condition 2 holds the join relation on generating slots is acyclic: a cycle of joins would give a return to a slot by concatenating the joining paths and an attaching edge path through each intermediate generator. The longest string $r$ is therefore finite and computable. Every 2-generator then has both attaching edge paths nonempty: an empty side makes its two object poles equal. Hence Response 93 applies. In each old inhabited temporal interval a reversed clique consists of simultaneously spatially composable slots, by its protected isolation. Its size is at most $r$. All old types from $\max(4,r+2)$ onwards are therefore already raw-inhabited over $B$. The truncation through $r+1$ suffices; for $r\le1$ use the no-separated-pair theorem. For $r\ge3$ the bare cube on a longest string forces a generator in degree $r+1$ by Response 29. For $r=2$ the two nonrepeatable slots give a missing raw square return in degree three; a fixed-2-skeleton extension needs a declaration at that degree. This proves optimality of the ceiling. The theorem does not require conservativity at types referring to the auxiliary generators. [Interval bound for positive rewrites](#researcher-response-93) · [Rank obstruction including repeated slots](#researcher-response-29) · [Nonrepeatable square case](#researcher-response-13)

## Researcher Response 101

**Every old raw judgment in global degrees four and five is decidable on every finite positive Gray 3-computad.** Both temporal sides of each declared 3-generator must be nonempty. Generating 2-cells can have empty edge paths, repeats and arbitrary spatial overlaps. The strict local 3-cells between any prescribed local 2-faces form an effectively finite set. In particular the reverse of a contextual generating triple or polygon-interval prism has no raw filler, even with other positive polygons and unrestricted spatial triples present.

Use the positive polygon comparison at prescribed faces in Response 8. The local 3-atoms are three intervals, or a polygon and an interval in either spatial order. Start with a parallel pair of local 2-faces $D,E$ at temporal input $u$. Give its occurrences mass one, transport masses at squares by the swap and at a polygon by equal sharing of its input sum. Use the height $h$ of Response 18, the sum over polygon occurrences of the total mass strictly preceding their input blocks. Every prism increases $h$ by the mass on the opposite interval. A triple preserves $h$, since its two faces transport the same three masses by the reversal and contain no polygon. The input-output mass function and the multiset of polygon labels are preserved throughout. Reject mismatches. With $c$ polygon occurrences and maximum polygon output length $m$ among them (one if none), every mass in any reading is at least $m^{-c}$. Thus, when $h(E)\ge h(D)$, at most $B=\lfloor (h(E)-h(D))m^c\rfloor$ prism steps can intervene. A prism changes the crossing count by at most $d=\max_P\big||P^+|-|P^-|\big|$ over the occurring polygons (zero if none). A triple preserves it. All intermediate readings therefore use at most $K=\#\mathrm{crossings}(D)+Bd$ squares and exactly $c$ polygons. [Polygon comparison](#researcher-response-8) · [Mass transport and prism signs](#researcher-response-18)

A second height distinguishes the triples. At each square, multiply the two crossing masses by the total mass strictly before the pair. Write $J$ for the sum of these products. Exchanging disjoint steps in a reading preserves $J$ because each step preserves total mass on its block. For a triple on temporal inputs of masses $a,b,e$, both faces cross the same three unordered pairs. Their external prefix contributions coincide. In the native word $121$ the middle crossing contributes the additional product $abe$; in $212$ the first and last crossings each contribute $abe$. Hence the target increases $J$ by exactly $abe$. Prefixes supply the same masses and suffixes receive the same vector in this comparison. The pair $(h,J)$ strictly increases lexicographically in every nonidentity generating local 3-step in context. This excludes both asserted reverses. Between successive prism steps the increase in $J$ per triple is at least $m^{-3c}$, while $0\le J\le K|u|^3$. There are at most $B+1$ such stretches. These bounds apply equally when successive crossings reuse the same strands.

At the fixed input, readings with at most $K+c$ local 2-steps are effectively finite. Each step chooses a temporal position and actual spatial slots in finite edge paths or an occurrence of a named polygon. Even empty edge paths have finitely many positions in the current path. Equality and the finite enumeration of contextual moves use the thin-context and factorization procedure of Response 18. At a fixed rank there are only finitely many tensor patterns of intervals and polygons, and divisions of a given spatial path into that many factors and stationary gaps are finite. The two heights now bound the length of *every* local 3-derivation between $D,E$, so the finite search also enumerates all strict fillers. For global degree five the input faces are parallel local 3-cells with common local 2-faces $D,E$. Every intermediate vertex is among exactly those enumerated fillers. Enumerate contextual local 4-steps at these vertices and test reachability, including the empty path. The global degree-five decision requires no bound on the number of local 4-pastes between such vertices. Response 8 transports both decisions to the original raw typings. Consequently surface failure in either degree is recursively enumerable on this whole class by enumerating surface derivations and checking their old boundaries.

## Researcher Response 102

**Raw inhabitation at every given old type of global degree at least four is decidable over an arbitrary finite positive Gray 3-computad.** More precisely, for each pair of parallel strict faces in that range one can enumerate the finite set of strict fillers. ## Researcher Response 103

**The universal gap test through degree three reduces to finitely many return problems on every finite positive Gray 3-computad without a spatial triple.** This includes polygons beside other events, with arbitrary temporal expansion and contraction and cycles in the object graph. In fact, if a nonempty bare gap has a return, that entire gap occurs as a contiguous subword of the *initial edge path* of one declared 3-rule. Hence an infinite language of middle paths for any pair forces a degree-three failure. For an interchange-containing binary surface the degree-three conservativity problem on this class is r.e.-complete. On *all* finite positive 3-computads the all-dimensional individual-context problem is a difference of two recursively enumerable sets, with no hypothesis on the object graph.

**Follow the first event.** On a fixed initial edge path $p$ form a finite directed graph. Its vertices are positioned occurrences of sources of 2-generators enabled on $p$. Give it an arrow from each event to each disjoint enabled event on its spatial left. For each occurrence of the initial edge path of a declared 3-rule in $p$, insert an arrow from the first event on its source list to the first event on its target list, translating both positions by the occurrence offset. These vertices exist by positivity. Every raw directed move on a nonempty history either preserves its first event or acts by an arrow of this graph. A generating exchange at the beginning promotes a disjoint left event. A polygon at the beginning uses its translated first-to-first arrow. All other moves act strictly after that event. Positivity also prevents a history from becoming empty. This observation is on the original fixed path $p$ even if a later intermediate path in the same history is much shorter. [Positioned history semantics](#researcher-response-2)

For a bare square take $p=s(a)\,m\,s(b)$. In the absence of a spatial triple all 2-generators have nonempty spatial sources, and **no enabled event can lie wholly inside $m$**: its name, preceded by $a$ and followed by $b$ with the indicated intervening path segments, would be a triple. Call an enabled event left if its source segment ends at or before the right end of $m$. Each left event starts strictly before $m$, while each other event ends strictly after it. Initially $LR$ has a left first event; the required $RL$ has another first event. A first-event path between them has a first departure from the left set. A native exchange only moves the first event spatially left and cannot do this. A polygon occurrence making the departure has its whole first source event and its whole first target event in its single *initial* edge-path window. That window starts before $m$ and ends after $m$, as asserted. The argument requires no edge of $m$ to survive later in any history.

Use the dictionary consisting of the empty word and the substrings of the finitely many declared initial windows. For each ordered pair of 2-generators test inclusion of its middle path language in the dictionary by the graph/trie product of Response 17. A missing path gives an explicit old failure at its square return. On success there remain only finitely many bare triples $(a,m,b)$ to check. Accessibility of the first event can still reject an individual return; when that necessary test passes, search the actual directed history relation for a return. The latter search can run indefinitely on a negative instance. All returns together are equivalent to degree-three conservativity by the bare-square criterion. This gives the r.e. upper bound, and the positive long-hom machine construction of Response 17 gives hardness already on an acyclic graph. If every rule is length-nonincreasing **or** every rule is length-nondecreasing, every successful bare return stays within two events. The polynomial dictionary, logspace substring test and two-event reachability algorithm of Response 17 then give NL-completeness in the explicit path/list presentation, now allowing the mixed polygons. Its length-preserving graph examples give the lower bound in both cases. [Bare squares and the dictionary algorithm](#researcher-response-17)

For the all-dimensional claim first reject spatial triples, which already force a degree-four failure here. On the other inputs, accepting all finitely many returns is an r.e. condition. Existence of a higher surface failure is also r.e. by the individual raw decision and enumeration of surface derivations. Taking the former set minus the latter proves the bound. A cycle on a path between the inner poles of a square gives infinitely many gaps and is always negative in the no-triple case, even if a short-hom polygon can repeatedly consume the loop. ## Researcher Response 104
**Empty ports in ordinary scalar rule contexts.** Take a point, generating $n$-scalars and directed $(n+1)$-generators between arbitrary raw scalar composites. A birth has no inputs and a death has no outputs. Count ports with multiplicity. For $n\ge3$ the following hold.

1. With arbitrary births and deaths, including declarations with neither inputs nor outputs, all eight binary and both published surfaces are conservative through degree $2n-1$.
2. With the same unrestricted ports, published insertion and binary $\{A,U\}$ also reflect degree $2n$ for $n\ge4$. At $n=3$ they reflect degree six whenever the named fixed-end arrow group is residually nilpotent, in particular for any antichain of uses.
3. If every rule has an output, published insertion and binary $\{A,U\}$ are conservative in **every** dimension. The same holds if every rule has an input. More generally, for a particular supported computation it suffices that each rule use has at least one port and that each birth is comparable by directed dependence with every death. This allows different choices of the common nonempty side on different intervals.

The all-dimensional assertion includes, for example, arbitrarily many simultaneous uses of a rule from the empty configuration to two equal colours, followed by arbitrary many-input, many-output rules. The published strict-unit theory and the smaller binary subsurfaces of $\{A,U\}$ inherit both insertion bounds. We give the occurrence and cut arguments explicitly because a configuration at a cut can be empty, and two different cuts can have the very same live wires.

### Naming events before wires

First use the occurrence pullback of Response 33 at **rank $n+1$**. Leave the entire $n$-skeleton in place and give each rule position in the surface witness a different copy of its rule, with the original attaching terms. The theorem applies to arbitrary lower attaching terms. It lifts both the surface witness and its literal raw faces using the same position assignments. At degree $n+1$ use the positions of the witness itself. At higher degrees use its iterated $(n+1)$-source. All $(n+1)$-faces then use the same named events once each, by the position bijections. Next apply the state lift of Response 38 at rank $n$. Give each initial scalar position its own wire name. For an event named $e$, fix orders on its input and output positions using the position model for the theory being tested. Its state function sends **every** tuple of input states to the list of fresh wire names $(e,1),\ldots,(e,q_e)$ at its output ports. Keep the rule copy indexed by its input tuple in the lifted computad. The family construction uses the function only in the forward direction. The empty input has one assignment, and the function to the assignments on an empty output is unique. Thus a birth retains its name even on an empty input, and a death declaration retains the tuple it consumed even on an empty output. The same argument works for a rule with no ports. The state lift again retains the old heads when lifting raw faces. [State lift for functions on position assignments](#researcher-response-38) · [Copies with several output ports](#researcher-response-78)

To see why the two lifts determine one network, sequentialize the ordinary strict $(n+1)$-image. The two lifts project to that history. Each initial name is present once, and each other wire name is created at most once because its event name can occur only once. Consequently no wire can be consumed twice. Above rank $n+1$ the strict value of the lifted witness is an iterated identity, so at the two arrow faces the counts of the **input-indexed rule declarations** agree. There is one copy per event use, hence its entire input tuple agrees at both faces. Its output names were fixed by its name and port order. This reconstructs the same incidence graph even when a whole component has disappeared before the last cut. The order induced by wire incidence is acyclic, since the sequential history is a linear extension. Keep precisely these wire and event declarations and the point. Their attaching types are supported there, and support restriction applies to the witness as well as to its literal faces. Folding sends any raw filler back to the given type. At degree $n+1$ a strict history gives a raw arrow by successively placing the rules at their sites and joining the configurations in each intervening pure component. The smaller degrees are covered by the pure skeleton. Transport of nonstandard point boundaries and of the pure port configurations works relative to the old boundary as in Responses 38 and 86, including the empty configuration, which is a point. Write $D$ for the finite set of named events. Grade arrows in the local $n$-fold hom by $\mathbb N^D$ using the ordinary strict event counts. Counts add under local composition. In the category with sheets, an object also has a vector $v\in\mathbb Z^D$ and an arrow of grade $d$ starting on $v$ ends on $v+d$. Higher cells have the sheets of their endpoints. Start at sheet zero with precisely the initial wires. End at sheet $\mathbf 1_D$ with the final wires. In any intervening cube string, nonnegativity forces exactly one jump of each name overall. A jump requires all its named inputs to be present. Inducting on a serial reading, the prefix is an ideal $I$ of the event poset and the live multiset is exactly the wires whose producer has fired, or is external, and whose consumer has yet to fire, or is external. We spell out how to use the spatial constraints of Responses 86 and 99 with the new cut formula. For marks take all maximal directed wire paths in the named network, including bypass wires. Here are details concerning spatial symbols in this diagram. A slot of a spatial paste is occupied if it contains a surviving **wire or use**, including in the interior of its local computation. For the bounds on a split symbol record its exterior divergences on traces in distinct slots, including traces starting or ending inside the interval. **Through degree three, individual-context Gray conservativity for every binary surface containing $I$ is $\Pi^0_2$-complete on finite positive 3-computads.** This holds with one loop edge, all 2-generators endomorphisms of single edges, and all 3-rules supported on one or two consecutive edges. Thus this is a classification of the bounded-degree question, whereas Response 103 gives the lower complexity of that question without triples and the difference bound for the all-dimensional problem.

Use the graph $x\xrightarrow f v\xrightarrow g z$ with an additional loop $h$ at $v$. Every site in an edge word is an edge occurrence. A mark at a site rewrites that edge to itself, so temporal histories have the same spatial path throughout. We use the following finite positive rules, spelled as directed list replacements. A travel rule on two adjacent sites is a polygon on the corresponding two-edge path between its literal positioned lists. Exchange rules at one site are declared polygons, since two tokens at that same edge cannot use a disjoint native exchange.

* There is an immobile mark $a$ at $f$. The immobile marks at $g$ are an inert $b$, delimiters, collecting and machine states, and tape symbols. At each of $f,h,g$ there are four other marks, denoted $+,-,P,C$. The first three can travel either way between adjacent sites by a unary-to-unary rule. Each of the four can commute in either temporal direction with any mark at its own site. No such rule exchanges two immobile marks.
* The scanner $C$ can travel one edge in either direction. A rightward crossing **into an $h$** produces a $+$ at its destination before the scanner. Traversing the same adjacency leftward produces a $-$ at that destination instead. Include the inverse of each of these list replacements, which consumes the indicated token to undo that trip. On an adjacency ending in $g$ the motion has zero cost in both directions. On $f h^n g$ the scanner potential at a site is the number of $h$ edges through that site, counted from the left. Its displacement always equals the change in signed token count $\#(+)-\#(-)$.
* At $f$ declare $a\to C_f$ and $P_f\to a$. At $g$ declare $C_g\to LIR$, where $L,R$ are distinct delimiters and $I$ the collecting state. The rule $+_g I\to I U$ consumes one positive token and inserts one unary input letter. A directed start rule changes the collector to the initial machine configuration, after which the program runs on the collected word. Its only successful exit cleans the delimited word to one $P_g$. There is no other way for the scanner to finish or for the program to produce a pass.

For a machine index $e$, use a deterministic tape program accepting unary $k$ exactly when machine $e$ halts on every input $i<k$. This is effective by interleaving the $k$ computations. Use the positive semi-Thue encoding of Response 17 at the one $g$ site: tape cells, one head-state, two end delimiters, the guarded extension at an end, and accepting cleanup to a single letter. All moves require the current state; choose the final cleanup rule to consume both extremities before producing $P_g$. In particular, on deletion of the mobile tokens and the inert $b$, a completed collecting phase followed by a successful run has consumed exactly some accepted $k$. Only the collector inserts $U$ as an input. During simulation there is no collector; no two stationary program letters can permute by a native square at $g$ or by a declared local commutation. Interposed mobile tokens can delay a rule or commute past it, but their deletion preserves each machine transition. A fixed universal program suffices, with the parameter written in the initial tape by the start rule. Thus even the 2-skeleton and the rest of the rule dictionary can be fixed. [Positive machine encoding](#researcher-response-17)

**Completeness of the square tests in a positive instance.** A freely travelling token commutes past any event on the same spatial path: bring it to the event, use its local commutation, and undo its travel in the other temporal position. For a scanner travel to the other site using the token-producing moves. Commute the entire resulting word past the other mark, using free travel for the emitted tokens and the local commutation for the scanner. Apply the inverse travel sequence to that word on the other side. This works from either temporal order, also for two scanners. Thus every bare pair with a mobile mark has a return. Two immobile marks can occur spatially separated only as $a$ on $f$ and one of the stationary marks on $g$. Suppose $n$ is accepted. In the temporal prefix consisting of $a$ alone, scan monotonically across $f h^n g$, producing $n$ positive tokens. Move them all to $g$, commute them into the collection window, and accept the unary word of length $n$. This produces $P_g$ in that prefix. Commute it past the stationary event, travel to $f$ and turn it back into $a$. All these are directed moves from the sorted to the unsorted layering. **Necessity for the designated pair.** Consider a return for $a,b$ on $f h^n g$. With no session starting at $a$ there is no first move: $a,b$ are immobile, the temporal order is already left first, and no program is active. Once $a$ is spent there is a single scanner, then a single delimited computation, then a single pass. Inductively a completed session returns to exactly one $a$, with possibly residual signed tokens and the inert $b$. There is no source of another scanner, computing state, or pass in that sector. A return must complete a positive number $r$ of sessions. In each, scanner moves change the signed count by exactly $n$ in total before its arrival at $g$, even with arbitrarily many reversals and inverse moves. All subsequent changes to that count are the $k_j$ positive tokens consumed for the session's accepted input. Initial and final signed counts are zero. Consequently
$$
                     rn=\sum_{j=1}^r k_j .
$$
The accepted unary language is downward closed, so if $n$ is rejected, every accepted $k_j$ is strictly less than $n$. This contradicts the equality. This accounting permits tokens to survive between sessions and does not assume that the program collected all tokens available in one visit. Hence the gap $h^n$ returns for the designated pair **exactly** when the first $n$ computations halt.

The set of indices of total machines is $\Pi^0_2$-complete: any predicate $\forall n\,\exists t\,R(e,n,t)$ with decidable $R$ is totality of the machine on $n$ searching for such a $t$. The construction gives the lower bound. For the upper bound enumerate all bare squares of the finite input and ask for each a finite directed return. Response 2 makes this exactly the surface property through degree three.
